The '''Epstein profile''', introduced by [[Paul Sophus Epstein]] in 1930<ref name="epstein1930">{{cite journal
 | last        = Epstein
 | first       = Paul S.
 | title       = Reflection of waves in an inhomogeneous absorbing medium
 | journal     = [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]
 | volume      = 16
 | issue       = 10
 | pages       = 627–637
 | year        = 1930
 | doi         = 10.1073/pnas.16.10.627
| doi-access = free
 | pmid = 16577283
 | pmc = 526706
 | bibcode = 1930PNAS...16..627E
 }}</ref>, is an exactly solvable mathematical model
for the vertical variation of the refractive index in a horizontally homogeneous,
vertically stratified medium.
In quantum mechanics, it is better known as the '''Eckart potential''' or
the '''hyperbolic Rosen–Morse potential'''.

The '''Epstein layer''' is a transition zone
described by this profile; typically it involves an absorbing medium.

==Definition and alternate names==

Let ''z'' be the coordinate normal to the layers and let
<math>\varepsilon(z)</math> denote the relative
[[permittivity]] — equivalently the squared refractive index, or in
[[Underwater acoustics|acoustics]] the squared inverse sound speed.
With the dimensionless depth

:<math>\zeta = z/L,</math>

Epstein's profile reads

:<math>\varepsilon(z) = \varepsilon_1
  + (\varepsilon_2-\varepsilon_1)\,\frac{e^{\zeta}}{1+e^{\zeta}}
  + \varepsilon_3\,\frac{e^{\zeta}}{\left(1+e^{\zeta}\right)^2},</math>

or equivalently

:<math>\varepsilon(z) = \frac{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2}{2}
  + \frac{\varepsilon_2-\varepsilon_1}{2}\,\tanh\frac{\zeta}{2}
  + \frac{\varepsilon_3}{4}\,\operatorname{sech}^2\frac{\zeta}{2}.</math>

The four parameters have a direct meaning:
<math>\varepsilon_1</math> and <math>\varepsilon_2</math> are the
bulk values below and above the transition layer;
<math>\varepsilon_3</math> adds a symmetric bump or dip centred on <math>z=0</math>;
and ''L'' sets the thickness of the transition region.
Epstein measured the thickness by the dimensionless number

:<math>s = kL = 2\pi L/\lambda ,</math>

with <math>k=2\pi/\lambda</math> the vacuum wavenumber, so that
''s'' is the layer thickness in units of
<math>\lambda/2\pi</math>.

The profile is monotonic if and only if
<math>|\varepsilon_3| \le |\varepsilon_2-\varepsilon_1|</math>;
otherwise <math>\varepsilon(z)</math> overshoots and passes through
an interior maximum or minimum whose value can be adjusted at will
through <math>\varepsilon_3</math>. Epstein regarded this
four-parameter family as "general enough" to approximate
essentially any transition occurring in applications while
retaining "the advantage of mathematical elegance and
rigor".<ref name="epstein1930"/>

In quantum mechanics, the very same potential has been introduced,
slightly before Epstein, by [[Carl Eckart]];<ref>{{cite journal
 | last        = Eckart
 | first       = Carl
 | title       = The penetration of a potential barrier by electrons
 | journal     = [[Physical Review]]
 | volume      = 35
 | issue       = 11
 | pages       = 1303–1309
 | year        = 1930
 | doi         = 10.1103/PhysRev.35.1303
| bibcode = 1930PhRv...35.1303E
 }}</ref>
it is referred to as the ''Eckart potential'' or
the ''hyperbolic Rosen–Morse potential'' (1932),<ref>{{cite journal|first1=N. |last1=Rosen |first2=P. M. |last2=Morse |title=On the Vibrations of Polyatomic Molecules |journal=Phys. Rev. |volume=42 |issue=2 |page=210 |year=1932 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.42.210|bibcode=1932PhRv...42..210R }}</ref>
not to be confused with the
[[trigonometric Rosen–Morse potential|''trigonometric'' Rosen–Morse potential]].

Two special cases carry their own names. The '''Epstein transition layer'''
with <math>\varepsilon_3=0</math> is a monotonic tanh step
from <math>\varepsilon_1</math> to <math>\varepsilon_2</math>. This is
the smooth counterpart of a sharp [[Fresnel equations|Fresnel]]
interface.

The '''symmetric Epstein layer''' with <math>\varepsilon_2=\varepsilon_1</math>
is a <math>\operatorname{sech}^2</math> bump or dip superimposed on a
homogeneous background.
In quantum mechanics, it is known as the [[Pöschl–Teller potential]].

==Exact solution==

===Reduction to the hypergeometric equation===

Epstein starts from the scalar wave equation
<math>\Delta\phi + k^2\varepsilon\phi = 0</math>. For electromagnetic
waves this scalar form is exact only in
[[Transverse mode|TE]] (''s''-polarized) geometry, where the electric
vector lies in the plane of the layers. The TM (''p''-polarized) case
carries an extra term <math>\varepsilon'/\varepsilon</math> and is not
reducible to hypergeometric form for the Epstein profile, although
Epstein expected the results to be qualitatively the
same.<ref name="epstein1930"/><ref name="lekner"/> For
[[Schrödinger equation|quantum particles]] and for acoustic waves in a
medium of constant density the scalar equation is exact.

Separating the coordinate ''x'' parallel to the layers by the ansatz
<math>\phi = e^{ikpx}\psi(z)</math>, where
<math>p=\sqrt{\varepsilon_1}\sin\theta_1</math> is the
[[Snell's law|Snell]] invariant, leaves the one-dimensional equation

:<math>\frac{d^2\psi}{dz^2}
  + k^2\bigl(\varepsilon(z)-p^2\bigr)\psi = 0 .</math>

Read as a stationary [[Schrödinger equation]], this is the same problem
with <math>\varepsilon</math> in the role of a negative potential,
which is why the profile recurs in quantum mechanics under the names
given above.

The substitution <math>u=e^{\zeta}</math> maps the equation into the
[[hypergeometric function|hypergeometric equation]], whose
[[monodromy]] group — the "circuit relations" connecting the solutions
at <math>z\to-\infty</math> with those at <math>z\to+\infty</math> — is
classically known. The reflection coefficient is a ratio of the
coefficients of that connection.<ref name="epstein1930"/>

===Reflection coefficient===

Introducing

:<math>a = is\,q_1,\qquad b = is\,q_2,\qquad
      d = \tfrac12 - \sqrt{\tfrac14+s^2\varepsilon_3},\qquad
      q_j = \sqrt{\varepsilon_j-p^2},</math>

where <math>k q_j</math> is the wavenumber component normal to the
layers in medium ''j'', the amplitude reflection coefficient of a wave
incident from the region <math>z\to-\infty</math> is

:<math>R = \frac{\Gamma(2a)\,\Gamma(d-a-b)\,\Gamma(1-d-a-b)}
                {\Gamma(-2a)\,\Gamma(d+a-b)\,\Gamma(1-d+a-b)} .</math>

The expression is invariant under <math>d\to 1-d</math>, so the choice
of branch for the square root in ''d'' is immaterial.

For a non-absorbing layer in which the wave propagates on both sides,
<math>q_1</math> and <math>q_2</math> are real, so that ''a'' and ''b''
are purely imaginary, <math>a=ia'</math> and <math>b=ib'</math> with

:<math>a' = s\,q_1,\qquad b' = s\,q_2,</math>

each being ''L'' times the corresponding normal wavenumber, and ''d''
is real. Using <math>\Gamma(x)\Gamma(1-x)=\pi/\sin\pi x</math>, the
reflectance collapses to the compact result

:<math>|R|^2 = \frac{\sin^2\pi d + \sinh^2\pi(a'-b')}
                    {\sin^2\pi d + \sinh^2\pi(a'+b')} .</math>

If <math>\tfrac14+s^2\varepsilon_3<0</math>, then
<math>d=\tfrac12-id'</math>, and <math>\sin^2\pi d</math> is to be
replaced by <math>\cosh^2\pi d'</math>.

Angle of incidence and wavelength enter only through <math>a'</math>,
<math>b'</math> and ''d''. The entire angular and spectral dependence
of the reflectivity is thus available in closed form, which makes the
Epstein profile a standard test case for approximate methods such as
the [[WKB approximation]] and the
[[Born approximation]].<ref name="brekhovskikh"/><ref name="lekner"/>

===Epstein transition layer===

For <math>\varepsilon_3=0</math> one has <math>d=0</math> and

:<math>|R|^2 = \frac{\sinh^2\pi(a'-b')}{\sinh^2\pi(a'+b')},\qquad
   1-|R|^2 = \frac{\sinh 2\pi a'\,\sinh 2\pi b'}
                  {\sinh^2\pi(a'+b')} .</math>

Three limits illuminate the physics.

'''Thin layer.''' For <math>s\to0</math> the hyperbolic sines may be
replaced by their arguments, and one recovers the Fresnel amplitude
of a sharp interface,
<math>|R| = |q_1-q_2|/(q_1+q_2)</math>. A transition much thinner
than <math>\lambda/2\pi</math> is therefore optically
indistinguishable from a discontinuity. The same limit holds for the
general profile, because <math>d</math> is then of order
<math>s^2</math>, so that <math>\sin^2\pi d</math> is of fourth order
in ''s'' and negligible beside the second-order
<math>\sinh^2</math> terms.<ref name="epstein1930"/>

'''Thick layer.''' For large ''s'',
<math>|R| \simeq \exp\bigl(-2\pi\min(a',b')\bigr) = \exp\bigl(-4\pi^2 L\,\min(q_1,q_2)/\lambda\bigr)</math>.
Reflection is suppressed ''exponentially'' as soon as the transition
extends over more than a wavelength. This is the quantitative form of
the familiar rule that gradual index changes do not reflect, and it
is the principle exploited in graded-index
[[anti-reflective coating|antireflection coatings]] and
[[rugate filter]]s.

'''Total reflection.''' If <math>\varepsilon_2<p^2</math>, then ''b''
becomes real, numerator and denominator of ''R'' turn into complex
conjugates, and <math>|R|=1</math> ''exactly''. A continuous layer
therefore obeys the same condition for
[[total internal reflection]] as a sharp interface, however thick the
transition.<ref name="epstein1930"/>
Together these results establish Epstein's conclusion: appreciable
reflection from a smooth layer occurs only near the condition of total
reflection, so that outside that regime the geometrical-optics
treatment of ionospheric ray paths is justified.

===Symmetric Epstein layer===

For <math>\varepsilon_2=\varepsilon_1</math> one has <math>a=b</math>
and

:<math>|R|^2 = \frac{\sin^2\pi d}
                    {\sin^2\pi d + \sinh^2 2\pi a'} .</math>

The reflectance vanishes identically — at ''all'' angles of incidence —
whenever ''d'' is an integer, that is whenever

:<math>s^2\varepsilon_3 = n(n+1),\qquad n = 0,1,2,\dots</math>

Since <math>n(n+1)\ge 0</math>, this requires a bump
(<math>\varepsilon_3>0</math>) and never occurs for a dip. Between the
zeros the reflectance oscillates, which Epstein described as the layer
showing "the colors of thin or of thick plates".<ref name="epstein1930"/>

The symmetric Epstein layer is therefore a family of ''reflectionless''
profiles. Its quantum-mechanical counterpart is the classical result
that the potential well
<math>V(x) = -\hbar^2 n(n+1)/(2mw^2)\,\operatorname{sech}^2(x/w)</math>
transmits particles of every energy without
reflection.<ref name="poeschlteller">{{cite journal
 | last1       = Pöschl
 | first1      = G.
 | last2       = Teller
 | first2      = E.
 | title       = Bemerkungen zur Quantenmechanik des anharmonischen Oszillators
 | journal     = [[Zeitschrift für Physik]]
 | volume      = 83
 | issue       = 3–4
 | pages       = 143–151
 | year        = 1933
 | doi         = 10.1007/BF01331132
| bibcode = 1933ZPhy...83..143P
 }}</ref><ref name="landau">{{cite book
 | last1       = Landau
 | first1      = L. D.
 | author-link = Lev Landau
 | last2       = Lifshitz
 | first2      = E. M.
 | title       = Quantum Mechanics: Non-Relativistic Theory
 | edition     = 3rd
 | publisher   = Pergamon Press
 | location    = Oxford
 | year        = 1977
 | at          = §25, problems
}}</ref>
Reflectionless <math>\operatorname{sech}^2</math> profiles occupy a
distinguished place in mathematical physics: they are the one-soliton
potentials of the [[Korteweg–De Vries equation]], the simplest output
of the [[inverse scattering transform]], and a standard example of a
[[Darboux transformation]] in
[[supersymmetric quantum mechanics]], in whose classification the
whole Epstein family is shape-invariant.

===Absorbing layers===

Epstein's own question concerned a ''conducting'' layer. He therefore
writes <math>\varepsilon_2=\kappa_2+i\Sigma_2</math> and
<math>\varepsilon_3=\kappa_3+i\Sigma_3</math>, "where
<math>\kappa</math> measures the refractive power and
<math>\Sigma</math> the conductive power of the medium", while
<math>\varepsilon_1</math> stays real because the wave originates in a
region free of conduction. The gamma-function formula for ''R'' remains
valid, but Epstein declined to discuss the general case, which he
judged "too cumbersome", and evaluated instead the two special cases
above, asymptotically for large ''s'' by
[[Stirling's approximation]].<ref name="epstein1930"/>

Two regimes emerge:

'''Weak conductivity.''' The transparent results are recovered
continuously: instead of total reflection one obtains <math>|R|</math>
slightly below unity, and away from the total-reflection condition
the reflectance stays exponentially small.

'''Strong conductivity.''' The reflectance tends to
<math>|R| = \exp(-\pi a')</math>, again exponentially small unless the
incidence is grazing or the layer is thinner than a wavelength.

The second result looks paradoxical, since strong conduction is usually
associated with high reflectivity, as in metals. Epstein resolved the
paradox by noting that in a ''continuous'' medium the reflected wave is
generated at all depths of the transition layer, and that the large
absorption prevents it from re-emerging with appreciable
intensity.<ref name="epstein1930"/> His overall conclusion was that in
radio propagation "if rays are reflected at all, their path can be
computed neglecting conductivity, as if the medium were transparent" —
the justification he had set out to obtain for the geometrical-optics
analysis of his preceding paper.<ref name="epstein1930a">{{cite journal
 | last        = Epstein
 | first       = Paul S.
 | title       = Geometrical optics in absorbing media
 | journal     = [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]
 | volume      = 16
 | issue       = 1
 | pages       = 37–45
 | year        = 1930
 | doi         = 10.1073/pnas.16.1.37
| doi-access = free
 | pmid = 16577262
 | pmc = 1075936
 | bibcode = 1930PNAS...16...37E
 }}</ref>

==Applications==

===Ionospheric physics===

The Epstein layer entered ionospheric physics through its originator's
motivation and through the dissertation of [[Karl Rawer]], who used it
to compute partial reflection and the apparent (virtual) height of
ionospheric layers.<ref name="rawer1939">{{cite journal
 | last        = Rawer
 | first       = Karl
 | title       = Elektrische Wellen in einem geschichteten Medium
 | journal     = [[Annalen der Physik]]
 | volume      = 427
 | issue       = 5
 | pages       = 385–416
 | year        = 1939
 | doi         = 10.1002/andp.19394270502
 | language    = de
}}</ref>
In present-day empirical modelling the name denotes above all the
''shape function'': electron-density profiles are synthesized from
superposed symmetric Epstein layers, one per ionospheric region, each
described by a peak density, a peak height and a thickness parameter,
connected where necessary by Epstein step
functions.<ref name="rawer1988">{{cite journal
 | last        = Rawer
 | first       = K.
 | title       = Synthesis of ionospheric electron density profiles with Epstein functions
 | journal     = [[Advances in Space Research]]
 | volume      = 8
 | issue       = 4
 | pages       = 191–199
 | year        = 1988
 | doi         = 10.1016/0273-1177(88)90239-6
| bibcode = 1988AdSpR...8d.191R
 }}</ref>
This construction underlies the bottomside and topside profiles of the
[[International Reference Ionosphere]] and of the related NeQuick
model.<ref name="bilitza2022">{{cite journal
 | last1       = Bilitza
 | first1      = Dieter
 | last2       = Pezzopane
 | first2      = Michael
 | last3       = Truhlik
 | first3      = Vladimir
 | last4       = Altadill
 | first4      = David
 | last5       = Reinisch
 | first5      = Bodo W.
 | last6       = Pignalberi
 | first6      = Alessio
 | title       = The International Reference Ionosphere model: A review and description of an ionospheric benchmark
 | journal     = [[Reviews of Geophysics]]
 | volume      = 60
 | issue       = 4
 | article-number       = e2022RG000792
 | year        = 2022
 | doi         = 10.1029/2022RG000792
| bibcode = 2022RvGeo..6000792B
 }}</ref>
The attraction of the construction, as against a piecewise assembly of
[[Chapman function|Chapman layer]]s or of constant-gradient segments,
is that a sum of Epstein terms stays analytic and differentiable
everywhere, so that the unphysically sharp transitions between altitude
regimes disappear on their own.<ref name="rawer1988"/>

===Acoustics and geophysics===

In [[underwater acoustics]] and in seismology the Epstein layer serves
as the canonical analytic model of a transition in sound speed — a
thermocline, a sediment layer, or a velocity gradient between two
half-spaces — and as the benchmark against which numerical propagation
codes and ray-theoretical approximations are
tested.<ref name="brekhovskikh">{{cite book
 | last        = Brekhovskikh
 | first       = L. M.
 | author-link = Leonid Brekhovskikh
 | title       = Waves in Layered Media
 | edition     = 2nd
 | publisher   = Academic Press
 | location    = New York
 | year        = 1980
}}</ref>
Note that <math>\varepsilon</math> corresponds to the squared inverse
sound speed, so that an Epstein layer in <math>1/c^2</math> is not an
Epstein layer in <math>c</math>.

===Optics and reflectometry===

Graded interfaces occur wherever two materials interdiffuse or a
surface is rough on a scale small compared with the wavelength.
Averaging a sharp interface over a Gaussian distribution of heights
yields an [[error function|error-function]] profile, for which no exact
solution of the wave equation is known, whereas the tanh profile has a
closely similar shape and is exactly solvable. Expanding the exact
result for a thin transition layer gives

:<math>|R| \simeq |R_\text{F}|\,\exp\bigl(-2k_{z1}k_{z2}\sigma^2\bigr),
  \qquad \sigma = \pi L/\sqrt3,\qquad k_{zj} = k q_j,</math>

which is the Névot–Croce attenuation factor of grazing-incidence
reflectometry.<ref name="nevot1980">{{cite journal
 | last1       = Névot
 | first1      = L.
 | last2       = Croce
 | first2      = P.
 | title       = Caractérisation des surfaces par réflexion rasante de rayons X. Application à l'étude du polissage de quelques verres silicates
 | journal     = Revue de Physique Appliquée
 | volume      = 15
 | issue       = 3
 | pages       = 761–779
 | year        = 1980
 | doi         = 10.1051/rphysap:01980001503076100
 | url = https://hal.science/jpa-00244786
 | language    = fr
}}</ref>
Here <math>\sigma</math> is exactly the [[root mean square|rms]] width
of <math>d\varepsilon/dz</math>. Since that factor depends on the
interface only through its second moment, the tanh and error-function
profiles agree to leading order whenever their widths are matched. The
Epstein layer therefore serves as the exactly solvable reference
against which the Névot–Croce approximation, and graded-interface
models in [[X-ray reflectivity|X-ray]] and
[[neutron reflectometry]] generally, can be
tested.<ref name="lekner">{{cite book
 | last        = Lekner
 | first       = John
 | title       = Theory of Reflection: Reflection and Transmission of Electromagnetic, Particle and Acoustic Waves
 | edition     = 2nd
 | publisher   = Springer
 | location    = Cham
 | year        = 2016
 | chapter     = Exact results
 | series = Springer Series on Atomic, Optical, and Plasma Physics
 | volume = 87
 | doi         = 10.1007/978-3-319-23627-8
| bibcode = 2016trrt.book.....L
 | isbn = 978-3-319-23626-1
 }}</ref>

==Generalizations==

Burman and Gould treated a ''generalized Epstein profile'' with an
additional parameter and obtained the reflection and transmission
coefficients in terms of hypergeometric functions of one and, in the
general case, two variables.<ref name="burman1965">{{cite journal
 | last1       = Burman
 | first1      = R.
 | last2       = Gould
 | first2      = R. N.
 | title       = The reflection of waves in a generalized Epstein profile
 | journal     = [[Canadian Journal of Physics]]
 | volume      = 43
 | issue       = 5
 | pages       = 921–934
 | year        = 1965
 | doi         = 10.1139/p65-088
| bibcode = 1965CaJPh..43..921B
 }}</ref>
Sluijter and Weenink extended the model to a magnetized plasma, an
Epstein density profile crossed by an inhomogeneous magnetic
field.<ref name="sluijter1966">{{cite journal
 | last1       = Sluijter
 | first1      = F. W.
 | last2       = Weenink
 | first2      = M. P. H.
 | title       = Wave propagation through an Epstein density profile across an inhomogeneous magnetic field
 | journal     = [[Physica (journal)|Physica]]
 | volume      = 32
 | issue       = 4
 | pages       = 741–748
 | year        = 1966
 | doi         = 10.1016/0031-8914(66)90006-1
| bibcode = 1966Phy....32..741S
 }}</ref>
More generally, Epstein-type profiles are a standard ingredient of
exactly solvable models in plasma physics.<ref name="ginzburg">{{cite book
 | last        = Ginzburg
 | first       = V. L.
 | author-link = Vitaly Ginzburg
 | title       = The Propagation of Electromagnetic Waves in Plasmas
 | edition     = 2nd
 | publisher   = Pergamon Press
 | location    = Oxford
 | year        = 1970
}}</ref>

==History==

Epstein's 1930 paper was the second of a pair. In the first he had
shown, by generalized geometrical optics, that conductivity distorts
ray paths only negligibly unless absorption is strong over one
wavelength.<ref name="epstein1930a"/> Geometrical optics, however, says
nothing about the ''reflected'' wave, and it was to close this gap that
he sought an exactly solvable profile. He chose the hypergeometric
equation because its monodromy group was the only one completely known,
and then constructed the most general dielectric profile that leads to
it.

Epstein reported that he had used a special case of the theory in his
lectures on differential equations since 1919, as a physical
illustration of analytic continuation — the law of reflection, he
wrote, furnishes "a physical visualization of the rather abstract
concept of analytical continuation" — demonstrating it by Wiener's
experiment on light propagating through a layer of water above one of
glycerine. He credited H. P. Robertson with working out another special
case.<ref name="epstein1930"/>

In 1933, physicists [[Gertrud Nordheim-Pöschl|Gertrud Pöschl]] and [[Edward Teller]] analysed the symmetric case as an
anharmonic-oscillator model.<ref name="poeschlteller"/> Rawer's 1939
dissertation work brought the profile into ionospheric
practice,<ref name="rawer1939"/> and the reviews in the monographs of
Brekhovskikh and Budden established it as a textbook
model.<ref name="brekhovskikh"/><ref name="budden">{{cite book
 | last        = Budden
 | first       = K. G.
 | author-link = Kenneth Budden
 | title       = The Propagation of Radio Waves: The Theory of Radio Waves of Low Power in the Ionosphere and Magnetosphere
 | publisher   = Cambridge University Press
 | location    = Cambridge
 | year        = 1985
}}</ref>
